extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide for respectful, accurate and inclusive usage of terms related to race, religion, disability, gender, sexuality, ethnicity and other identity topics, with pronunciation, capitalization and usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: pinoy/pinay
rubrics_metrics.description: Tagalog, meaning a Filipino man; pinay means woman.

rubrics_metrics.name: pink triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Now a gay pride symbol, it was the symbol gay men were required to wear in Nazi concentration camps during World War II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lesbians sometimes also use a black triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polock, Polack
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory word for a Pole or a person of Polish descent. The word derives from Polak, which means a Polish male or a person of Polish nationality, which has a neutral connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid; note historical usage (example: All in the Family).

rubrics_metrics.name: polyamorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in more than one consensual intimate relationship at a time, or being non-monogamous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with pansexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: polygamy
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of having more than one spouse at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual notes: practiced historically by Mormons (officially outlawed by LDS in 1890; members excommunicated today), permitted in Islam according to the Quran (men may marry up to four women if they can be 'equally just').

rubrics_metrics.name: post-racial
rubrics_metrics.description: A controversial term that describes a society that’s devoid of racial preference, discrimination and prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: An anxiety disorder that can develop after traumatic events such as military combat, natural disasters, terrorist incidents, serious accidents, traumatic brain injury, physical and sexual assault in adults or children, and any other traumatic experience. PTSD can be diagnosed a month or more after the traumatic event has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having PTSD only if the information is relevant to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a reputable source. Use 'Post-traumatic stress disorder' on first reference and 'PTSD' on second. 'Flashback' may denote reliving an event that triggered PTSD.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty line, poverty threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents the level of income deemed adequate to live in a particular place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. Federal Poverty Level is calculated yearly by HHS and used to determine eligibility for federal programs; poverty lines are typically anchored to minimum nutritional requirements plus a modest allowance for non-food needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fines and fees for petty violations such as fare-hopping on public transit, playing loud music, speeding, driving with a suspended license or expired registration, zoning violations for unkempt property, wearing 'saggy pants,' and failure to appear in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: powwow
rubrics_metrics.description: A celebration and social gathering honoring sacred American Indian traditions through dancing, drumming, singing and the gathering of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only when referring to the title of a specific American Indian event. Avoid for a general gathering because the term evokes a stereotypical image. Comes from the Narragansett word for shaman; may honor an individual or special occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: practicing (LGBTQ+)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide advises avoiding this term to describe someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'sexually active' as a modifier when public awareness of an individual’s behavior is germane.

rubrics_metrics.name: pre-lingually deaf / postlingually deaf / late-deafened
rubrics_metrics.description: Prelingually deaf refers to individuals born deaf or who became deaf prior to learning to speak a language. Postlingually deaf or late-deafened describes a person who lost hearing after learning to speak a language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are acceptable, although explanation may be required for a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: preferred pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the term 'preferred pronouns.' Someone’s pronouns are not a preference; the term is only appropriate when someone uses more than one set of pronouns and has a preference for one over the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead use: 'pronouns.' (Updated March 2021)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride Day
rubrics_metrics.description: Short for gay/lesbian pride, commonly used to indicate celebrations commemorating the Stonewall Inn riots of June 28, 1969.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride events typically take place in June. See Stonewall.

rubrics_metrics.name: primitive
rubrics_metrics.description: A potentially insulting term to describe a person or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using this term.

rubrics_metrics.name: pro-choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people who support abortion rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because views are nuanced, journalists should instead use 'pro-abortion rights' or a similar precise description.

rubrics_metrics.name: pro-life
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used to describe people who oppose abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because views are nuanced, journalists should instead describe views specifically, such as 'opposed to abortion' or 'against abortion rights.'

rubrics_metrics.name: progressive
rubrics_metrics.description: A term that emerged to refer to people of faith who are liberal-to-moderate in political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is disputed because it implies other groups are regressive; use carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: projects, the
rubrics_metrics.description: Common shorthand for low-income housing projects that can carry a negative connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral terms like 'low-income housing project' or 'public housing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: If sources share a transgender or gender-nonconforming identity on the record, ask which pronouns they use and incorporate them. 'They/them/their' are acceptable as singular nonbinary pronouns if the subject uses them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity for the audience is paramount. If gender identity is not relevant and a nonbinary pronoun could confuse, explain that the subject uses a nonbinary pronoun or recast for clarity. Avoid 'preferred pronouns' or 'chosen pronouns.' Use forms like 'Sanchez, who uses the pronoun they' or 'Sanchez, whose pronouns are they/them/their.' Be aware of rolling pronouns and that some people use different pronouns on different days; if confused, ask. (Updated March 2023)

rubrics_metrics.name: proselytize
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of seeking converts to a faith; many Christian groups distinguish proselytizing (unethical coercive methods) from evangelizing (pressure-free presentation of faith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'proselytize' unless it is being used in a negative context. Prefer 'evangelism' (Protestant) or 'evangelization' (Catholic/Orthodox).

rubrics_metrics.name: psycho
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'crazy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid; colloquial and offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: psychotic/psycho
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad term for symptoms of certain mental health problems (delusions, hallucinations, loss of contact with reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'psychotic' and 'psychosis' only when they accurately describe a medical experience. Avoid using 'psychotic' to describe a person—refer instead to a person as having a psychotic condition or psychosis. Avoid colloquial usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puerto Rico
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States; Spain ceded it to the U.S. in 1898, and Puerto Ricans were made U.S. citizens in 1917. In 1952 Puerto Rico voted to become a commonwealth, which did not fundamentally change U.S. relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punjab
rubrics_metrics.description: Both a state in north India and a province in eastern Pakistan; partition divided Punjab. The name means 'five waters' or 'five rivers' referring to the rivers draining the region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punjabi
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary language of Punjab and one of the main regional languages in India. A person from Punjab is referred to as a Punjabi.

rubrics_metrics.name: qawwali
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotional songs of the Sufi tradition of Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'kuh-WAH-lee.' Do not capitalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: quadriplegia / quadriplegic
rubrics_metrics.description: Quadriplegia is paralysis of all four limbs and the torso, often caused by spinal cord or brain injury; paraplegia is similar but does not affect the arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People-first language preferred: 'a person with quadriplegia' rather than 'quadriplegic.' If someone self-identifies as 'quads,' use in quotes. (NCDJ)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal name is the Religious Society of Friends; 'Quakers' can be used in all references. Members typically refer to themselves as Friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically considered Christian; some are nontheistic. Worship and business gatherings are called 'meetings.' Titles such as elders or ministers are capitalized when used before a name.

rubrics_metrics.name: queen
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally a pejorative term for an effeminate gay man but often used acceptably as slang among LGBTQ people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offensive when used as an epithet; use only if there is a compelling reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: queer
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally pejorative, appropriated by some LGBT people as a self-affirming umbrella term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not universally accepted; avoid unless describing someone who self-identifies that way or in a direct quote. In 'LGBTQ', Q typically means queer and/or questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: quinceañera
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hispanic celebration of a girl’s 15th birthday, signifying transition from youth to adulthood; both a social and religious event often beginning with a mass followed by a reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'keen-see-nyair-ah.' Historically signified readiness for marriage; contemporary meanings may vary and include events for sons in some families.

rubrics_metrics.name: quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific or presubscribed number that must be met to reach a certain goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used in affirmative action debates but is not synonymous with affirmative action (which is a broader practice or program aimed at correcting discrimination and diversifying institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quran
rubrics_metrics.description: The holy book of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the direct word of God as dictated in Arabic to Muhammad by the Angel Gabriel beginning about 610 to about 632.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'ku-RAHN.' 'Quran' is the preferred spelling and is capitalized in all references. Use 'Koran' only if it is part of a specific title or name.

rubrics_metrics.name: rabbi
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebrew word for teacher and the title used by Jewish clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize before a name on first reference; on second reference use only the cleric’s last name.

rubrics_metrics.name: race
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s race should not be mentioned unless relevant; this applies also to ethnicity, sexual orientation and religion. Derogatory terms or slurs may not be used unless directly relevant to the news and then only with senior editor approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stereotypes. Examples of relevance: Crime stories—detailed suspect descriptions may include skin color when properly attributed; biographical stories—reserve race/ethnicity for significant, historic or 'first' achievements so as not to overemphasize race over ability. See also ethnicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: race card, 'play the race card'
rubrics_metrics.description: To say someone is 'playing the race card' is to accuse them of injecting race into a discussion, often to deflect, diminish or discredit concerns about race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expression trivializes discussions of racism and can act as backlash against talk about race; use with caution and awareness of its implications (cite bell hooks commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: race, U.S. Census definitions of
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau adheres to 1997 OMB standards on race and ethnicity, classifying written responses into categories such as White, Black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander. Reporting of more than one race is permitted and responses are based on self-identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions include geographic/origin examples for each category (e.g., 'White' includes origins in Europe, the Middle East or North Africa; 'Asian' includes origins in Far East, Southeast Asia or the Indian subcontinent).

rubrics_metrics.name: rainbow flag
rubrics_metrics.description: A flag of six equal horizontal stripes (red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet) symbolizing the diversity of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramadan
rubrics_metrics.description: Islam’s holy month during which Muslims fast from sunup to sundown, commemorating the revelation of the Quran to Muhammad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'rah-mah-DAHN.' The end of Ramadan is marked by Eid al-Fitr. Ramadan follows a lunar calendar and shifts each year in the Western calendar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rashomon
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally a short story ('In a Grove') by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, adapted into the acclaimed 1950 film 'Rashomon', which explores differing eyewitness memories of the same crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguably the most influential work of fiction on modern journalism; 'Rashomon' (Japanese for 'castle gate') is a dilapidated area in Kyoto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rastafarians
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a political and religious movement among blacks in Jamaica and other countries; belief in Haile Selassie as messiah and a worldview including repatriation to Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on rituals: use of marijuana as a holy herb, chanting, reggae music as movement's popular music. Origins trace to 1930s and figures like Marcus Garvey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Period after the Civil War (generally 1865-1877) in which attempts were made to rebuild the South and address political, social, and economic problems from readmission of Confederate states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructionist Judaism
rubrics_metrics.description: A 20th-century movement founded by Rabbi Mordechai Kaplan that views Judaism as a social rather than God-centered phenomenon; Reconstructionists generally do not consider Hebrew Scriptures divinely inspired and are less hierarchical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstructionist rabbis are ordained at the Reconstructionist Rabbinical College in Wyncote, Pa.

rubrics_metrics.name: recovery, treatment (mental illness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recovery from mental illness is a process through which individuals improve health and wellness, live self-directed lives, and strive to reach full potential; mental illness is treatable and recovery possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize diagnosis is not forever; sharing stories of recovery or successful management helps reduce misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: red
rubrics_metrics.description: A good-luck color in several cultures, including Indian and Chinese; favored for weddings and traditional for the bindi.

rubrics_metrics.name: redlining
rubrics_metrics.description: A discriminatory practice that denies financial services to residents of certain areas based on race or ethnicity, seen in systematic denial of mortgages, insurance and loans based on location rather than individual qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term originates from lenders and government literally drawing a red line on maps around neighborhoods deemed unworthy of investment; historically affected Black neighborhoods most heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: redneck
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory term for whites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use.

rubrics_metrics.name: redskin
rubrics_metrics.description: An overtly racist term comparable to the N-word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid. The Native American Journalists Association urges news outlets to limit use of racial team names and images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redskins (NFL team)
rubrics_metrics.description: History of the NFL team formerly known as the Washington Redskins: under pressure, the team announced review and retired the name in 2020, temporarily using 'Washington Football Team'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on long-standing calls to change the name, public pressure, sponsor actions (e.g., FedEx), and references to further reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: rehab
rubrics_metrics.description: See treatment/treatment center/rehab center/detox center.

rubrics_metrics.name: relationships (LGBTQ+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesbian, gay and bisexual people use various terms to describe their commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask individuals which term they prefer; if not possible, 'partner' is generally acceptable. See husband, wife, lover, partner.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious left
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to describe people of faith with liberal political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists can use it but should specify which groups and what actions are being referred to.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious right
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to describe people and groups whose religious beliefs inform their conservative political and social views; dates to 1979 with the Moral Majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should refer to 'religious right' or 'religious conservatives' but should specify which groups are meant and what they are promoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on capitalization, usage and customs for religious titles across major traditions (Baptist, Buddhism, Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Eastern Orthodox, Jehovah's Witnesses, Judaism, Nation of Islam, Pentecostalism, Protestant churches, Quakers, Roman Catholic Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rules include not using 'Dr.' before clergy for academic doctorates unless academic credentials are important; capitalize titles before a name and lowercase otherwise; nuances for specific faiths (examples and rules provided for each tradition).

rubrics_metrics.name: reparations
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments or measures intended to right past wrongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical U.S. examples: $1.5 billion to settle claims by Black farmers (Pigford v. Glickman), $1.6 billion to Japanese Americans interned during WWII and various payments to Native Americans (e.g., $3.4 billion settlement in 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian reservations are areas of land reserved by the U.S. government as permanent tribal homelands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. reservation policy dates to 1787; in 2015 there were 326 reservations and about 56 million acres in reservations and trust land; more than 60% of American Indians live away from reservations.

rubrics_metrics.name: residential care homes
rubrics_metrics.description: Homes offering personalized services to small groups of adults who live together, providing lodging, meals and assistance with daily living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other terms include adult family homes, board and care homes, or personal care homes.

rubrics_metrics.name: retarded
rubrics_metrics.description: See mentally retarded, mentally disabled, intellectually disabled, developmentally disabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid; use people-first and less pejorative terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: reverse discrimination, reverse racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases used in lawsuits and accusations that affirmative action disadvantages men and non-minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research indicates this is rare; example: 1995 Brandeis study found few such cases and limited relief ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roma, Romany, Romani
rubrics_metrics.description: Roma (Romani or Romany) are a traditionally itinerant ethnic group, primarily in Europe but with branches elsewhere; often called 'Gypsies' but that term has negative connotations and many Roma do not identify with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spellings and subgroup distinctions noted (Romany often refers to Romanichals in England); evidence suggests origins in northern India; distinguish Roma from Irish Travelers who are distinct despite similar itinerant lifestyles. Note history of persecution including by Nazis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman Catholic Church
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest Christian community in the world and in the U.S.; considers itself the full expression of the church founded by Jesus Christ, traces origins to Church of Rome and exercises papal primacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on sacraments (seven), organizational structure (Holy See, Vatican, archdioceses, dioceses), papal naming conventions and historical fractures with Eastern Orthodoxy and Protestantism.
